FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Re: Nature and People First Arizona PHS, LLC
Chilchinbeto Pumped Storage Project
Project No. P-15419-000



November 4, 2026

Dear Secretary,

Nature and People First Arizona PHS, LLC (“NPFA” or the “Applicant”) respectfully submits this
letter regarding its pending application for a preliminary permit for the Chilchinbeto Pumped Storage
Hydropower Project (the “Project”) and two related filings submitted on July 27, 2026:

   1. The Motion to Intervene filed jointly by Tó Nizhóní Ání (“TNA”), Diné Citizens Against
      Ruining Our Environment (“Diné C.A.R.E.”), Black Mesa Trust, and the Center for Biological
      Diversity; and
   2. The supplemental comments accompanying that Motion to Intervene, filed by TNA, Diné
      C.A.R.E., and Black Mesa Trust.

NPFA respects organizations that voice concerns and raise questions regarding its Chilchinbeto
pumped storage hydropower project and has done so since the very beginning of its engagement in the
development of this project more than six years ago. The company has met on several occasions with
parties expressing concerns and raising questions about the Project to listen to their views, answer
their questions, and provide clarification when necessary. However, NPFA wishes to clarify several
important points in response to statements and allegations made by these organizations in their filings.

Clarification of the support NPFA received from the Resources and Development
Committee (RDC), the Navajo Nation Council committee responsible for overseeing
infrastructure projects

NPFA achieved a very significant milestone on May 19, 2025, when the RDC voted 4 to 1 to “accept
NPFA’s report,” meaning that 80% (EIGHTY PERCENT) of the voting members voted in favor of
accepting the report. This milestone should not be downplayed. It represented a major step forward in
securing institutional support from one of the highest-level Navajo Nation institutions responsible for
reviewing infrastructure projects. The level of support was overwhelming.

This meant that 80% of the voting members agreed to allow NPFA to file an application for a FERC
Preliminary Permit, as the company had specifically requested this authorization in its report to the
RDC. The September 2, 2025, letter from the Navajo Nation Department of Justice (“DOJ”),
confirming that the Navajo Nation did not object to NPFA filing a FERC Preliminary Permit
application, was a direct result of the RDC’s vote to accept NPFA’s report.
 NPFA has never claimed that this vote represented more than that, but it certainly did not represent
less than that either.

Navajo Nation attorney Brandon Bitsuie of Drummond Woodsum has also confirmed this fact in the
attached letter. In his letter, Mr. Bitsuie also clarifies the role of the Navajo Nation Department of
Justice as the sole official voice of the Navajo Nation when it comes to expressing an opinion on a
project such as the Chilchinbeto PSH Project. He further explains that, because the Navajo Nation is
responsible for a significant portion of the permitting process, the Navajo Nation DOJ cannot commit
to supporting the Project regardless of its final design and characteristics.

The Project has received considerable institutional support from communities
directly impacted by the Project, starting with the community of Chilchinbeto

The Chilchinbeto Chapter has adopted four resolutions supporting NPFA’s Project over the past five
years, all without a single opposing vote. NPFA has also received numerous favorable resolutions
and letters of support from several other Navajo Nation chapters, grazing officials, and regional
institutions.

NPFA has received supporting resolutions or letters of support from the following chapters, regional
organizations, and local officials. These documents are attached:

   •   The Chapters of Kayenta (85% support), Oljato (100% support), and Ts’ah Bii Kin (100%
       support).
   •   The four Chapters of the NOST Regional Council (Navajo Mountain, Oljato, Shonto, and
       Ts’ah Bii Kin) - 100% support
   •   The Western Navajo Agency Council, representing 18 Chapters (69% support) in the broader
       region of the project.
   •   Navajo Nation Council Delegate Shaandiin Parrish, representing the Navajo Chapters most
       impacted by the project (Chilchinbeto, Kayenta, and Dennehotso).
   •   The District 8 Grazing Officials, representing four Chapters (Chilchinbeto, Dennehotso,
       Oljato, and Kayenta) most impacted by the project with 100% support.
   •   Permission to Survey granted by the Navajo Nation General Land Department Division on
       May 14, 2024, and renewed on May 19, 2026.

It is particularly important to highlight the very significant September 2023 vote in favor of the Project
at a Western Navajo Agency Council meeting, representing 18 chapters, including the Chilchinbeto
Chapter and several neighboring chapters. This demonstrated that support for the Project extended
throughout the region, well beyond the Chilchinbeto Chapter alone. It is also important to note that,
during this meeting, Tó Nizhóní Ání (TNA) attempted to secure the adoption of a resolution opposing
the Project. That resolution was rejected.

In addition, NPFA has signed agreements with grazing permittees granting access to the land required
for the Project, covering nearly 5,000 acres at the top and bottom of Black Mesa in the Chilchinbeto
area. These agreements have been approved by the Navajo Nation and led to NPFA obtaining a Land
Withdrawal from the Navajo Nation for the Project on August 21, 2025.

Reasons for the very strong institutional support from communities directly impacted
by the Project

The strong support the Project has received from communities directly impacted by it can be explained
by several compelling and practical considerations.
 NPFA has devoted considerable time over the years to meeting with communities throughout the
Western Navajo Nation and in the capital, Window Rock, to introduce the Project in detail, listen to
questions and concerns, better understand Navajo culture and the challenges of daily life in the Navajo
Nation, and adjust the Project to provide meaningful benefits to local communities.

As a result, a large number of Navajo citizens and elected officials have expressed strong support for
NPFA’s Project over the years because it will deliver significant benefits and help address some of the
most fundamental challenges facing the Navajo Nation today:

   •   The lack of well-paying jobs within the Navajo Nation, which forces people to leave their
       communities, separates families, and weakens Navajo culture and language. The Project will
       create 1,000 jobs during construction, 100 direct and indirect jobs afterward for 100 years, and
       potentially as many additional induced jobs in the local community. This is particularly
       significant for a community such as Chilchinbeto, which has suffered greatly from the closure
       of the local coal mines operated by Peabody Western Coal Company.
   •   The lack of water for livestock, which requires residents to haul water over long distances
       almost every day—an exhausting, costly, and polluting undertaking. Water shortages for
       livestock have become so severe that the Navajo Nation is advising ranchers to reduce the size
       of their herds, thereby reducing their sources of income. Ranching is an integral part of Navajo
       culture, and being forced to gradually abandon this way of life because of water scarcity is
       deeply painful and costly for many Navajo people.
   •   The lack of water for growing livestock feed, which prevents local ranchers from producing
       enough hay to feed their animals, forcing them to purchase expensive hay and transport it over
       long distances, adding further costs and pollution. Center-pivot irrigation would allow ranchers
       to grow their own hay locally, reducing costs and improving their self-sufficiency.
   •   The lack of water needed to help mitigate the effects of climate change. NPFA intends to
       reserve 1% of the water in its reservoirs for firefighting, enough to support operations by the
       most powerful firefighting helicopters for approximately 155 days per year, seven hours per
       day. NPFA also plans to make water available to wildlife on Black Mesa, thereby helping
       improve local biodiversity once the Project has been built. In fact, NPFA has already held
       discussions on this subject with members of a conservation group living on Black Mesa.
   •   The need for additional revenue for the Navajo Nation to help address budget shortfalls
       resulting from the closure of the coal mines and the Navajo Generating Station, and to fund
       urgent priorities, particularly in healthcare and education.

These benefits are largely related to the fact that the Project is as much a water infrastructure project
for the local community as it is an energy project designed to help stabilize Arizona’s electric grid.
Some of these benefits are illustrated in the attached 3D rendering of the Project.

The Project will likely use the C Aquifer and unlock access to this aquifer for the local community.
Accessing the C Aquifer in Chilchinbeto is challenging for local residents because of its depth and the
slight salinity of its water. The Project therefore presents a unique opportunity for the local community
to gain access to the C Aquifer for the first time.

After the first two years, during which the reservoirs will be filled, the Project will require only 30%
of the water infrastructure’s pumping capacity to replenish water lost through evaporation. This will
free up significant pumping capacity to meet community needs, including livestock watering, farming,
wildfire suppression, and providing water for wildlife during periods of drought.

In addition, a number of Navajo Nation elected officials understand that the Navajo Nation is
underutilizing the C Aquifer and should strengthen its water rights by making somewhat greater use of
this resource in a reasonable and responsible manner.
 The C Aquifer is a vast groundwater reservoir containing approximately 400 million acre-feet of water
and receiving significant natural recharge, estimated at 290,000 acre-feet per year. This recharge
continues to occur, as illustrated by the significant flooding experienced throughout the region over
the past several weeks.

More than 60% of the C Aquifer lies within the Navajo Nation, yet only approximately 1% of annual
groundwater pumping from the aquifer takes place within the Navajo Nation. NPFA’s Project will
likely increase the Navajo Nation’s share to approximately 2% and will account for approximately
0.5% of annual recharge after the first two years and 0.04% of the total estimated volume of the C
Aquifer over 100 years, without taking natural recharge into account.

Communities located outside the Navajo Nation make extensive use of the C Aquifer for municipal
water supplies, industrial projects, and energy projects in particular. Some neighboring communities
have ambitious data center projects that will also use water from the C Aquifer. In addition, the federal
government has asked the State of Arizona to reduce its withdrawals from the Colorado River by 27%.

A number of Navajo Nation elected officials understand that they will need to defend their rights to
access the C Aquifer in this context and that making use of this water resource is probably the most
effective way to strengthen those rights.

TNA’s continued opposition to NPFA’s Project has generated frustration among a
number of Navajo Nation elected officials

It appears that TNA’s continued opposition to the Chilchinbeto PSH Project has generated significant
frustration among some local elected officials and residents who would be directly impacted by the
Project, unlike TNA’s leadership, particularly in light of what they perceive as inconsistencies in
TNA’s positions.

Paul Madson, who was serving as President of the Chilchinbeto Chapter in 2025, published an op-ed
in the Navajo Times in June 2025 in which he clearly expressed his frustration with TNA for the
following reasons. His op-ed is attached.

First, there is frustration over TNA’s opposition to a clean-energy project that would create well-
paying local jobs, particularly because TNA advocated for a just economic transition when it
supported the closure of the local coal mine. Several Chilchinbeto residents lost their jobs as a
consequence of the decline and closure of coal-related activities, and they understandably hope that
TNA will remain consistent with its commitment, still stated on its website, to support a just transition
and economic opportunities for communities affected by the transition away from coal.

Second, there is frustration over TNA’s opposition to the use of the C Aquifer in Chilchinbeto. TNA’s
leadership is based in Flagstaff, a community located 170 miles from Chilchinbeto, outside the Navajo
Nation, that would not be directly impacted by the Project.

In addition, 60% of Flagstaff’s municipal water comes from the C Aquifer, and its residents have
ready access to basic services such as laundromats. The situation in Chilchinbeto is very different as
the Chilchinbeto community has no access to the C Aquifer that is deep under the Chilchinbeto
Chapter.

Residents often have to haul water over long distances for ranching and other basic needs, which is
both burdensome and expensive. During the pandemic, for example, the lack of access to a local
laundromat made something as basic as washing clothes extremely difficult for residents, as they were
 subject to lockdown restrictions in Chilchinbeto and the nearest laundromat was located in Kayenta,
25 miles away.

Local residents also want greater access to water to help address the consequences of climate change,
including the increasing risk of wildfires and insufficient water supplies for livestock and wildlife,
particularly during increasingly frequent periods of severe drought.

They therefore have difficulty understanding why an organization that advocates for environmental
justice, and whose own community already makes extensive use of the C Aquifer, would actively
oppose efforts that could improve their access to water for their basic needs and create economic
opportunities in one of the poorest communities in the United States, where unemployment exceeds
90%.

Their frustration is further compounded by the perception that an organization receiving substantial
financial support from wealthy foundations, including Silicon Valley billionaires and donors outside
the Navajo Nation, is working to prevent projects that most local residents and elected officials believe
could materially improve their economic circumstances and quality of life.

For families struggling every day to make ends meet, these issues are not theoretical. They concern
jobs, water, economic opportunity, and the future of their communities.

Respectfully submitted,

Nature and People First Arizona PHS, LLC




Denis Payre

CEO Nature and People First

Re:      Docket No. P-15419-000

Dear Mr. Payre:

        On December 19, 2025, Nature and People First Arizona PHS, LLC (”NPF”) submitted
its Application for Preliminary Permit: Chilchinbeto Pumped Storage Project to the Federal
Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”), Docket No. P-15419-000. The Navajo Nation filed a
motion to intervene in the matter.1 The motion to intervene was filed by the Navajo Nation
Department of Justice (“NNDOJ”) through attorneys within the NNDOJ. The NNDOJ has such
authority under Navajo law and should be seen by FERC as the official position of the Navajo
Nation. In its motion, the Navajo Nation does not oppose the project or the issuance of the
preliminary permit but only asserts that it has interests that may be impacted by the project. On
May 19 2025, the Resources and Development Committee (“RDC”) of the Navajo Nation
Council voted 4 to 1 to accept a report NPF submitted to the RDC regarding the project, meaning
that 80% of the voting members voted in favor of accepting NPF's report. In this report, NPF
requested that the Navajo Nation not object to NPF’s filing of an application for a FERC
Preliminary Permit. This vote subsequently led to the issuance of the NNDOJ’s letter of support,
dated September 2, 2025, for NPF to reapply for a preliminary permit.2

        The NNDOJ is a department within the Navajo Nation Executive Branch.3 The NNDOJ
is headed by the Attorney General (“AG”) who is appointed by the Navajo Nation Council, upon
the recommendation of the Navajo President.4 The Navajo AG serves at the pleasure of the
Navajo Nation Council.5 This appointment and confirmation process provides the Attorney
General with a degree of institutional independence from the President. The Navajo AG reports
and is responsible to the Navajo Nation Council through the President for the accomplishment of
the purposes and objectives of the legal needs of the Navajo Nation.6 Further, the Navajo AG
represents the Navajo Nation government regarding its legal interests in the Nation’s dealings
and relations with all persons and organizations outside the Navajo Nation government.7 The

Navajo AG is the Chief Legal Officer of the Navajo Nation and has the charge of all legal
matters in which the Navajo Nation government has an interest.8 As such, the Navajo AG has the
authority to “defend and initiate all actions … in which the Navajo Nation is a party…”9

         The Navajo Nation is the ultimate decision maker in whether a lease will be granted
within its territory and therefore is a necessary party to this process.10 The Navajo Nation does
not oppose the project but it is also responsible for a significant portion of the permitting process.
Several Navajo Nation departments will need to ensure that the project complies with the Navajo
Nation’s applicable laws and regulations.11 The Navajo Nation therefore necessarily is reserving
its rights and cannot commit to supporting the project unconditionally, regardless of its final
design and characteristics.



Sincerely,
Brandon K. Bitsuie
Attorney
